\section{Find depth when the point lies on a known plane}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:find-depth-when-the-point-lies-on-a-known-plane}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:lec03-ray-plane}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
One pixel supplies a ray, not a distance. A known plane supplies the missing condition: \sphinxstylestrong{keep moving along the ray until you reach the plane}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sources:} lecture PDF pages 3–12; Spring 2020 Quiz 2, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s20\_quiz2.pdf}}, P1–P2, PDF page 1; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532f15\_quiz9.pdf}}, P1, PDF page 1, printed \sphinxstylestrong{Spring 2019 Quiz 9} despite the filename.


\subsection{First, keep the two kinds of coordinates straight}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:first-keep-the-two-kinds-of-coordinates-straight}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:ex-lec03-ray}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 3.3 — two points on one viewing ray}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} Spring 2020 Quiz 2, P1–P2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The camera center is the origin. A scene point is \(A=(X,Y,Z)^T\) and the virtual image plane is at \(f=Z/10\), with \(Z>0\). Where does the ray meet that plane?

\sphinxAtStartPar
A point along the ray is \(a=\lambda A\). Its third coordinate must be \(f\), so
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\lambda Z=Z/10\quad\Rightarrow\quad\lambda=1/10,
\qquad a=(X/10,Y/10,Z/10)^T.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(A=(2,1,20)^T\) and \(f=2\), the intersection is \(a=(0.2,0.1,2)^T\). It is one tenth of the distance along the same ray.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The quiz also asks for \(A\times a\). Since \(a=A/10\),
\(A\times a=(A\times A)/10=\mathbf0\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why zero is correct:} here \(A\) and \(a\) are ordinary \sphinxstylestrong{Euclidean 3D vectors} from the camera center. A zero cross product confirms parallel directions. They are not two homogeneous 2D image points being joined into a line. Same three\sphinxhyphen{}entry shape, different meaning.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Intersect the ray with a plane}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:intersect-the-ray-with-a-plane}}
\index{Ray–plane intersection@\spxentry{Ray–plane intersection}!Axial depth@\spxentry{Axial depth}}\ignorespaces
\sphinxAtStartPar
Suppose the known plane is \(AX+BY+CZ+D=0\). Here \(A,B,C\) are plane coefficients, not the point named \(A\) in the previous example. Work entirely in the \sphinxstylestrong{camera frame}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The image coordinate \((x',y')\) lies on a virtual plane at focal length \(f\). These three values use the same physical length unit. The ray direction with third component one is
\(q=(x'/f,y'/f,1)^T\). If you start with a pixel \((u,v)\) instead, first obtain \(q=K^{-1}(u,v,1)^T\) under the pinhole model; correct distortion before this step when necessary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A scene point at axial depth \(Z\) is \(P=Zq\). Substitute its coordinates into the plane:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
A\frac{Zx'}f+B\frac{Zy'}f+CZ+D=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
Z\left(A\frac{x'}f+B\frac{y'}f+C\right)=-D.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — depth from a ray and a plane}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:eq-lec03-ray-plane}
\begin{split}\gamma=(A,B,C)\,q,\qquad
Z=-\frac{D}{\gamma}
 =-\frac{Df}{Ax'+By'+Cf},\qquad P=Zq.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Require \((A,B,C)\ne\mathbf0\) and \(\gamma\ne0\). \(Z\) is \sphinxstylestrong{axial depth}, not Euclidean range. For dimensionless normal coefficients and \(D\) in meters, \(Z\) is in meters. Rescaling the plane coefficients leaves the result unchanged.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Recover a 3D point on the known plane}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} a calibrated image coordinate and plane coefficients in the camera frame.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Form \(q\) with third component one. Compute \(\gamma=(A,B,C)q\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(\gamma\ne0\), calculate \(Z=-D/\gamma\) and \(P=Zq\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check:} substitute \(P\) into the plane and reproject it. For a point visible in front of this camera, require \(Z>0\).

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Near\sphinxhyphen{}parallel rays amplify input errors. Judge this using the angle between the ray and plane, rather than an unnormalized denominator.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.850\linewidth]{{ray-plane}.pdf}
\caption{A side view of Example 3.4. The image\sphinxhyphen{}plane intersection fixes the ray; the scene\sphinxhyphen{}plane intersection fixes its depth. The \(Y\) coordinate is suppressed only in the drawing.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:fig-lec03-ray-plane}}\end{figure}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:ex-lec03-plane}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 3.4 — put numbers into the depth answer}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} printed Spring 2019 Quiz 9, P1, whose requested symbolic answer is \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:eq-lec03-ray-plane}. The following numbers are an original companion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Given:} plane \(X+Z=10\), \(f=2\), \((x',y')=(0.5,0.25)\), all lengths in the same unit.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Plane coefficients: \((A,B,C,D)=(1,0,1,-10)\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ray: \(q=(0.25,0.125,1)^T\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Denominator: \(\gamma=1(0.25)+0(0.125)+1=1.25\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Depth: \(Z=10/1.25=8\); point \(P=(2,1,8)^T\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check the plane: \(2+8=10\). Check projection: \((fX/Z,fY/Z)=(0.5,0.25)\).

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The point is eight units forward along the optical axis. Its distance from the camera is \(\sqrt{2^2+1^2+8^2}=\sqrt{69}\), a little larger.

\end{TextbookBox}

\section{Recover a genuinely projective homography}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice:recover-a-genuinely-projective-homography}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice:lec03-dlt-practice}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The earlier DLT example recovered a shifted, stretched rectangle. This one adds a \sphinxstylestrong{changing denominator}: a square becomes a trapezoid, and its center does not map to the average of the destination corners.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} original numerical companion to lecture PDF pages 34–45, addressing the DLT/SVD priority in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ExamToDo.md}}. Use the canonical {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{DLT rows and SVD procedure}}}}; this section follows those steps with complete projective data.

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice:ex-lec03-dlt}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 3.5 — normalize, solve, and recover}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Given:} the following four exact correspondences, in the same order.


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxstyletheadfamily
\sphinxAtStartPar
Source \((u,v)\)
&\sphinxstyletheadfamily
\sphinxAtStartPar
Destination \((u',v')\)
\\
\sphinxmidrule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((0,0)\)
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((0,0)\)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((1,0)\)
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((2,0)\)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((1,1)\)
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((2,1)\)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((0,1)\)
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((0,2)\)
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{1. Normalize each image independently.} For the source square, centroid \((0.5,0.5)\) and mean radius \(1/\sqrt2\) give scale \(2\). For the destination, centroid \((1,0.75)\) and mean radius \(1.28288937\) give scale \(1.10236596\). Thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
T=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&-1\\0&2&-1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T'\approx\begin{pmatrix}1.102366&0&-1.102366\\0&1.102366&-0.826774\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The destination mean radius is the average of \(1.25,1.25,\sqrt{1.0625},\sqrt{2.5625}\). This is \sphinxstylestrong{mean distance}, not root\sphinxhyphen{}mean\sphinxhyphen{}square distance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{2. Fill the normalized DLT rows.} For the first pair,
\(\widetilde x=(-1,-1,1)^T\) and \(\widetilde x'\approx(-1.102366,-0.826774,1)^T\).
Its two rows, using \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture02/estimation:eq-lec02-dlt}, are approximately
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
(&-1,-1,1,0,0,0,-1.102366,-1.102366,1.102366),\\
(&0,0,0,-1,-1,1,-0.826774,-0.826774,0.826774).
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The other three pairs supply six more rows. The stacked matrix \(\widetilde A\) is \(8\times9\) with rank eight.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{3. Read the full right null vector.} A full SVD returns a \(9\times9\) right\sphinxhyphen{}vector basis. One unit null vector, rounded here, is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
h\approx(0.627538,0,0.209179,-0.156884,0.418359,-0.052295,
0.189755,0,0.569265)^T.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Its negative is equally valid. Reshape \sphinxstylestrong{row by row}, then rescale for display so the last entry is one:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\widetilde H\approx\begin{pmatrix}
1.102366&0&0.367455\\
-0.275591&0.734911&-0.091864\\
1/3&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Request the full basis: the eight singular values returned for an \(8\times9\) matrix do not themselves include a ninth listed zero. The extra right vector supplies its exact nullspace.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{4. Undo normalization.} Apply \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture02/estimation:eq-lec02-normalize}, using unrounded numbers in the calculation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H=(T')^{-1}\widetilde H T
\ \sim\ \begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\0&2&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{5. Check a corner and a point you did not fit.} For \((1,1)\), the homogeneous result is \((4,2,2)^T\), hence \((2,1)\): correct. The unmeasured square center gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H(1/2,1/2,1)^T=(2,1,3/2)^T
\quad\Rightarrow\quad (u',v')=(4/3,2/3).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
That differs from the destination vertex average \((1,3/4)\). Perspective does not preserve ordinary averages. The nonzero \(h_{31}\) makes the denominator depend on \(u\).

\end{TextbookBox}

\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice:use-the-matrix-to-make-an-image}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/homographies::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{court\sphinxhyphen{}rectification example}}}} is the slide deck’s real\sphinxhyphen{}image application, repeated here on PDF page 22. Its {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/warping::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{inverse\sphinxhyphen{}warping procedure}}}} tells you how to fill output pixels after estimating \(H\). Keep the directions separate: the matrix above sends source coordinates to destination coordinates; filling a destination pixel requires the reverse map.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Probability and the pentagon puzzle}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:probability-and-the-pentagon-puzzle}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:lec03-ransac-practice}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{How many random tries are enough?} First ask what counts as a successful try. RANSAC’s trial budget depends on that definition and on how samples are drawn.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sources:} lecture PDF pages 46–55; Fall 2025 Quiz 1, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532f25\_quiz\_1\_solution.pdf}}, Q1–Q2, PDF page 1; Spring 2019 Quiz 3, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s19\sphinxhyphen{}quiz3.pdf}}, P1’s four bullets, PDF page 1. The general RANSAC algorithm and trial\sphinxhyphen{}count formula remain in {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{Lecture 2}}}}.


\subsection{Start with the coin quiz}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:start-with-the-coin-quiz}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:ex-lec03-probability}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 3.6 — a winning streak, then repeated attempts}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} Fall 2025 Quiz 1, Q1–Q2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Q1:} You must win three independent fair coin flips in a row. Each flip has win probability \(1/2\), so one complete attempt succeeds with probability
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}q=(1/2)^3=1/8.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Q2:} Make one independent attempt each day for seven days. What is the probability of at least one successful day?

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is easier to count \sphinxstylestrong{no wins}. Each day fails with probability \(7/8\). All seven days fail with probability \((7/8)^7\). Subtract from one:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P(\text{at least one win})=1-(7/8)^7\approx0.607304=60.73\%.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Seven attempts do not give probability \(7/8\): that addition counts overlapping success events repeatedly. The complement calculation handles all possible numbers of wins at once.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Connection:} a RANSAC hypothesis needs several good matches together, just as this attempt needs several wins together. Repeating hypotheses then uses the same “one minus all failures” reasoning. The quiz’s geometry questions are solved in {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture01/frames-quizzes::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{Lecture 1}}}}.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Five corners, twenty\sphinxhyphen{}five possible matches}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:five-corners-twenty-five-possible-matches}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assume two pictures show only a generic irregular pentagon. All five corners are detected, but their identities are unknown. The quiz asks you to try \sphinxstylestrong{every possible pairing}.

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:ex-lec03-pentagon}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 3.7 — count matches and budget the search}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} Spring 2019 Quiz 3, P1, first three bullets.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Putative matches:} each of five source corners can pair with any of five destination corners: \(5\times5=25\) candidate pairs.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Correct matches:} relative to the intended homography, one partner per source corner is correct: five pairs. The inlier fraction is \(w=5/25=0.2\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Minimal homography sample:} four nondegenerate correspondences. Under the usual independent\sphinxhyphen{}match approximation, a clean sample has probability \(q=w^4=0.0016\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Choose confidence:} the question does not give one. Taking \(p=0.99\) and applying \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture02/estimation:eq-lec02-ransac} gives

\end{enumerate}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
N=\left\lceil\frac{\log(0.01)}{\log(1-0.0016)}\right\rceil
=2876.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpretation:} under this model, 2,876 trials give about a 99\% chance of drawing at least one all\sphinxhyphen{}inlier sample. This does not guarantee a correct final homography: samples must also be nondegenerate, and scoring must distinguish the intended model.

\end{TextbookBox}

50\%
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
72
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(1-(1-0.5^4)^{72}=99.04\%\)
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A single experiment can succeed or fail. Across many independent experiments, the observed success fraction tends toward the predicted probability; it need not equal it exactly. A clean sample is a sampling event, not proof of a correct model.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.850\linewidth]{{ransac-probability}.pdf}
\caption{More inliers can reduce the required trial count dramatically. The vertical axis measures sampling success, not geometric accuracy.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:fig-lec03-probability}}\end{figure}

\par\medskip


\subsection{More trials cannot solve a symmetry}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:more-trials-cannot-solve-a-symmetry}}
\index{Symmetry ambiguity@\spxentry{Symmetry ambiguity}}\ignorespaces \phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:ex-lec03-symmetry}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 3.8 — replace the shape with a regular pentagon}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} Spring 2019 Quiz 3, P1, final bullet.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A regular pentagon has five rotations that map its corner set onto itself. It also has five reflections. Composing the true image homography with any of these symmetries gives another homography supported by all five corners.
\begin{itemize}
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With no orientation restriction, there are \sphinxstylestrong{ten equally supported corner alignments}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If an external orientation constraint rules out reflections, \sphinxstylestrong{five rotations} remain.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A visible distinctive mark, corner identity, or other asymmetric evidence can break the tie. More random samples of the same unlabeled corners cannot.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 20\% inlier rate is measured relative to \sphinxstylestrong{one selected alignment}. Do not combine the ten alignments into one larger consensus: they are different models.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source wording:} the quiz calls a regular pentagon “equilateral.” Equal side lengths alone do not imply equal angles or these ten symmetries. This answer assumes a genuinely \sphinxstylestrong{regular} pentagon, as the question names it.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.850\linewidth]{{pentagon-symmetry}.pdf}
\caption{The numbers are explanatory labels, not visible features in the quiz images. The identical outlines cannot tell you which ordering is intended.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:fig-lec03-pentagon}}\end{figure}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{What does your confidence actually mean?}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Before quoting “99\%,” finish the sentence: “a 99\% chance of drawing at least one \_\_\_, under the sampling assumption \_\_\_.” If your answer says “a 99\% chance the reconstruction is right,” you have claimed more than the calculation supports.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxstepscope

\section{TLDR}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/tldr:tldr}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/tldr:lec03-tldr}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/tldr::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Lecture 3 in one sentence:} use camera geometry to solve concrete calibration and depth problems, then distinguish a probable clean sample from an identifiable correct model.


\subsection{The important things}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/tldr:the-important-things}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{FOV determines horizontal focal length only after stating the model.} A centered 640\sphinxhyphen{}pixel\sphinxhyphen{}wide, 90° pinhole view gives \(f_x=320\) pixels. Square pixels, zero skew, and a centered principal point supply the remaining assumptions for the quiz’s \(K\). See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/calibration::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{calibration}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pixel focal length is not physical focal length.} Multiply by physical pixel pitch to change units. The principal point is \((c_x,c_y)\) in pixels but \((0,0,f_{\rm phys})\) on the positive virtual image plane.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A scaled Euclidean 3D vector stays on the same camera ray.} The image\sphinxhyphen{}plane intersection is one tenth of the scene vector when \(f=Z/10\). Its cross product with that vector is zero. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{the ray quiz}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A known plane can supply missing depth.} Use \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:eq-lec03-ray-plane}, then check plane incidence, reprojection, and positive depth. A parallel ray may have no intersection or lie entirely in the plane.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Projective mappings do not preserve coordinate averages.} The fitted trapezoid’s mapped center differs from the average of its corners. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{normalized DLT walkthrough}}}} shows all the numerical stages.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Count the complement when attempts repeat.} The coin quiz gives \(1/8\) per attempt and \(1-(7/8)^7\approx60.73\%\) across seven independent attempts. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{probability}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{State the sampler before quoting a RANSAC budget.} The pentagon has 25 candidate pairs and five correct pairs for one alignment. The standard independent\sphinxhyphen{}status approximation gives 2,876 trials for 99\%; exact finite\sphinxhyphen{}pool rules give different counts.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Symmetry is missing information.} An unlabeled regular pentagon permits ten corner alignments without orientation constraints. More trials cannot select the intended one; extra asymmetric evidence can.

\end{enumerate}

\newpage


\subsection{Short quiz}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/tldr:short-quiz}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These original questions test this chapter’s applications.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A centered pinhole image is 800 pixels wide with 90° horizontal FOV. What is \(f_x\)? Does that alone determine \(f_y\)?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(f_x=400\) pixels and pixel pitch is \(0.004\,\mathrm{mm/pixel}\), where is the principal point on the positive virtual image plane in camera\sphinxhyphen{}frame millimeters?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a scene vector \((3,2,30)^T\) and \(f=3\), what is its image\sphinxhyphen{}plane 3D intersection? What is the cross product of the two vectors?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A ray is \(P=Z(0.5,0,1)^T\) and the known plane is \(X+Z=12\). Find \(Z\) and \(P\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
What happens if a ray has \(\gamma=0\) for a plane with \(D\ne0\)?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For Example 3.5’s matrix, where does source point \((0.5,0.5)\) go? Is it the destination vertex average?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If one independent attempt succeeds with probability \(1/4\), what is the chance of at least one success in three attempts?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A regular pentagon gives several equally supported alignments. Will increasing RANSAC’s trial count identify the intended alignment? Name evidence that could.

\end{enumerate}


\subsection{Answers}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/tldr:answers}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Show answers and short explanations}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{400 pixels.} Use \(800/(2\tan45^\circ)\). Vertical focal length needs an additional pixel\sphinxhyphen{}shape or calibration assumption.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\((0,0,1.6)\,\mathrm{mm}\).} Multiply \(400\) by \(0.004\); pixel principal\sphinxhyphen{}point coordinates are a different description.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\((0.3,0.2,3)^T\); zero cross product.} The intersection is one tenth of the scene vector.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\(Z=8\), \(P=(4,0,8)^T\).} Substitute into the plane: \(0.5Z+Z=12\). The depth is positive.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{No finite intersection.} The ray is parallel to a plane that does not contain the camera center.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\((4/3,2/3)\).} Divide \((2,1,3/2)^T\) by its last coordinate. It differs from the vertex average \((1,3/4)\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\(1-(3/4)^3=37/64\approx57.81\%\).} Subtract the probability of three failures from one.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{No.} A distinctive visible mark, a labeled corner, or other asymmetric scene evidence can distinguish models that have identical corner support.

\end{enumerate}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\chapter{Lecture 4: Two views reveal depth}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/index:lecture-4-two-views-reveal-depth}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/index:lecture04}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/index::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A one\sphinxhyphen{}pixel mistake can move a reconstructed point by centimeters—or much more. Why?} Two views turn image matches into 3D geometry, but the result depends on finding the right match and measuring its position accurately.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This chapter adds the assigned epipolar quizzes, noisy matrix estimation, calibrated pose recovery, stereo depth/error calculations, and dense matching. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{two\sphinxhyphen{}view introduction}}}} already owns distortion correction, epipoles, the fundamental constraint, and rectification; use those explanations as prerequisites.

\section{Solve the epipolar quizzes}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice:solve-the-epipolar-quizzes}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice:lec04-epipolar-practice}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{fundamental\sphinxhyphen{}matrix box}}}} gives the rule. These questions test whether you can use it without confusing a \sphinxstylestrong{point}, a \sphinxstylestrong{line}, and a \sphinxstylestrong{scalar constraint}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sources:} lecture PDF pages 18–21; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532f15\_quiz4.pdf}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s19\_quiz4.pdf}}, P1–P2, PDF page 1, both printed Spring 2019 Quiz 4; Fall 2025 Quiz 2, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532f25\_quiz\_2\_solution.pdf}}, Q1–Q2, PDF page 1.


\subsection{A symbolic matrix is still a calculation}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice:a-symbolic-matrix-is-still-a-calculation}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice:ex-lec04-symbolic}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.1 — expand the assigned constraint}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} Spring 2019 Quiz 4, P1–P2. The two filenames contain the same questions; use the second as a closed\sphinxhyphen{}notes retest.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{P1:} Let \(x_A=(x,y,w)^T\). Write the rows of \(F_{AB}\) as \(f_1^T,f_2^T,f_3^T\), where each \(f_i\) is a three\sphinxhyphen{}entry column vector. The line in image B is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\ell_B=F_{AB}x_A=
\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}x+f_{12}y+f_{13}w\\
f_{21}x+f_{22}y+f_{23}w\\
f_{31}x+f_{32}y+f_{33}w\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}f_1^Tx_A\\f_2^Tx_A\\f_3^Tx_A\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Those are \sphinxstylestrong{line coefficients}. If \(\ell_B=(a,b,c)^T\), an ordinary candidate \((u_B,v_B)\) must satisfy \(au_B+bv_B+c=0\). There is generally a whole line of candidates. For the requested sketch, draw the known point in A and the predicted line in B, as in the existing schematic \hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:fig-lec02-epipolar}]{Fig.\@ \ref{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:fig-lec02-epipolar}}} (a rectified special case).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{P2:} Substitute \(x_A=(1,0,1)^T\) and \(x_B=(0,1,1)^T\). First multiply by \(x_A\): this adds columns 1 and 3 of \(F\). Left multiplication by \(x_B^T\) then adds entries 2 and 3:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}x_B^TF_{AB}x_A=f_{21}+f_{23}+f_{31}+f_{33}=0.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In vector\sphinxhyphen{}product form this is
\(\bigl(f_2+f_3\bigr)^T x_A=0\), equivalently \(x_B\cdot(F_{AB}x_A)=0\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check:} the final result is one scalar, not a three\sphinxhyphen{}entry point.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Use two views to predict a point in a third}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice:use-two-views-to-predict-a-point-in-a-third}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice:ex-lec04-third-view}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.2 — two predicted lines meet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} Fall 2025 Quiz 2, Q1. The following numbers are an original companion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given \(x_A\leftrightarrow x_B\), generate two lines \sphinxstylestrong{in image C}:
\(\ell_A^C=F_{AC}x_A\) and \(\ell_B^C=F_{BC}x_B\). Their homogeneous intersection is
\(x_C\sim\ell_A^C\times\ell_B^C\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, take normalized image coordinates
\(x_A=(1/2,3/4,1)^T\), \(x_B=(1/4,3/4,1)^T\), and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
F_{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-1\\0&0&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
F_{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-1\\0&0&-1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiply: \(\ell_A^C=(-1,0,1/2)^T\), \(\ell_B^C=(-1,-1,1)^T\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Intersect: their cross product is \((1/2,1/2,1)^T\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check: both line dot products are zero. Thus \((u_C,v_C)=(1/2,1/2)\).

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These matrices are compatible: aligned cameras at \((0,0,0)\), \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\) observing point \((2,3,4)\) produce these image coordinates. The calculation predicts a location, but image evidence must still confirm that the point is visible there.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.750\linewidth]{{third-view}.pdf}
\caption{Two independent line predictions locate the third\sphinxhyphen{}image point. This applies the incidence operations from Lecture 1 to a new three\sphinxhyphen{}view task.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice:fig-lec04-third-view}}\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check the intersection before dividing:} coincident lines give a zero cross product and no unique prediction. Distinct parallel lines meet at an ideal point, not a finite pixel. With noise, nearly parallel lines give an unstable location; incompatible matrices or an incorrect A–B match can also spoil the prediction.


\subsection{Check the supplied matrix before trusting its name}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice:check-the-supplied-matrix-before-trusting-its-name}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice:ex-lec04-invalid-f}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.3 — correct the supplied solution}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} Fall 2025 Quiz 2, Q2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The question supplies \(x'=(1,2,1)^T\) and
\(F=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&2\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}\).
It asks for an epipolar\sphinxhyphen{}consistent \(x\).
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiply the row: \(x'^TF=(2,4,6)\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The required condition is \sphinxstylestrong{\(x'^TFx=0\)}, hence \(2u+4v+6w=0\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a finite point with \(w=1\), choose \(v=0\), giving \(u=-3\). Thus \(x=(-3,0,1)^T\) works. Another choice is \((-5,1,1)^T\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check directly: \((2,4,6)(-3,0,1)^T=0\).

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Two source issues:} the solution writes \(x'^TF=x\), equating a line row with a point. Its final line equation is usable, but that equality is wrong. Also, \(\det F=4\), so the supplied matrix has rank three and cannot be a genuine fundamental matrix for two pinhole cameras.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These points satisfy the \sphinxstylestrong{given bilinear equation}; the matrix still cannot describe valid camera geometry.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Estimate F from noisy matches}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation:estimate-f-from-noisy-matches}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation:lec04-estimation}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{eight\sphinxhyphen{}point route}}}} already supplies the linear rows and normalization order. Here we add what makes that route usable: a numerical noisy fit, an explicit rank constraint, and an error measured in pixels.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} lecture PDF pages 24–37; printed slides 24–34, then 39–41. The section develops the earlier Hartley–Zisserman–Pollefeys material.


\subsection{Make the fitted matrix physically admissible}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation:make-the-fitted-matrix-physically-admissible}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Noise usually gives a full\sphinxhyphen{}rank linear estimate. A true fundamental matrix must have rank two.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — nearest rank\sphinxhyphen{}two correction}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/estimation:eq-lec04-ranktwo}
\begin{split}\widehat F=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)V^T,
\qquad
F_2=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,0)V^T.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(3\times3\) SVD has \(\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\sigma_3\ge0\). This minimizes the Frobenius distance (the square root of the sum of squared entry differences) among matrices of rank at most two. Require \(\sigma_2>0\) for rank \sphinxstylestrong{exactly} two. It does not minimize image reprojection error.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Correct the normalized estimate}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} the matrix reshaped from the normalized linear system’s smallest right singular vector.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute its SVD and set only the smallest singular value to zero.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Undo point normalization using the existing rule \(F=T'^TF_2T\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check:} rank two, valid epipoles, and pixel\sphinxhyphen{}space errors on matches you did not fit.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Normalization improves numerical conditioning; it cannot repair outliers or degenerate geometry. The source’s image\sphinxhyphen{}size mapping to \([-1,1]^2\) is a scaling heuristic. The worked example uses independent centroid/mean\sphinxhyphen{}distance normalization from Lecture 2.

\end{TextbookBox}

\Needspace{15\baselineskip}


\subsection{Measure how far a point misses its predicted line}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation:measure-how-far-a-point-misses-its-predicted-line}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An algebraic residual \(x'^TFx\) changes if you rescale \(F\). Pixel distance to the line does not.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — point\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}line and symmetric epipolar error}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/estimation:eq-lec04-epipolar-error}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{dist}(x',\ell')&=\frac{|au'+bv'+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}},\quad
x'=(u',v',1)^T,\ \ell'=(a,b,c)^T,\\
r&=x'^TFx,\quad \ell'=Fx,\quad \ell=F^Tx',\\
e_{\rm sym}^2&=r^2\left[\frac1{\ell_1'^2+\ell_2'^2}
+\frac1{\ell_1^2+\ell_2^2}\right].
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use undistorted pixel coordinates and finite lines with nonzero first\sphinxhyphen{}two\sphinxhyphen{}component norm. The symmetric error sums squared distances in both images; it is not the same as minimizing jointly corrected image positions. Near an epipole, a vanishing line makes this calculation undefined.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Score a hypothesis in image units}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Predict a line in each image and compute its perpendicular point distance.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Combine the two squared distances if using the symmetric criterion.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set a threshold in units matching that criterion: pixels for distance, pixels squared for squared error.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inspect held\sphinxhyphen{}out errors and spatial coverage, not just the number of fitted points.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For line \((0,-2,6)^T\) and point \((5,4,1)^T\), the distance is \(|-8+6|/2=1\) pixel. Scaling the line by ten leaves the answer unchanged.

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation:ex-lec04-eightpoint}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.4 — a complete noisy eight\sphinxhyphen{}point\sphinxhyphen{}route fit}\par\smallskip

Coordinates are pixels, rounded to two decimals \sphinxstylestrong{before fitting}.

\subsection{Robust fitting: change the model and sample size}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation:robust-fitting-change-the-model-and-sample-size}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the existing {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{RANSAC explanation}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{sampling qualifications}}}}. The new detail is that a fundamental\sphinxhyphen{}matrix \sphinxstylestrong{seven\sphinxhyphen{}point solver} can generate multiple candidate matrices from one sample. Its two\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional linear nullspace becomes \(F(\lambda)=F_0+\lambda F_1\); imposing \(\det F(\lambda)=0\) gives a cubic, generically with one or three real candidate roots. Score each candidate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An eight\sphinxhyphen{}point solver needs eight matches instead. At 80\% inliers and 99\% clean\sphinxhyphen{}sample confidence, the independent\sphinxhyphen{}status budgets are \sphinxstylestrong{20} trials for seven\sphinxhyphen{}point samples and \sphinxstylestrong{26} for eight\sphinxhyphen{}point samples. The slide’s table on PDF page 35 corresponds to about \sphinxstylestrong{95\%}, not 99\%; choose the confidence explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After scoring, refit on the inliers, search near predicted epipolar lines for additional matches, and refine geometric error. Under Gaussian image\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate noise, the slide’s maximum\sphinxhyphen{}likelihood recommendation minimizes squared displacements to jointly corrected corresponding image points; this is stronger than finding the nearest matrix in entry space. PDF page 36’s ±1.5\sphinxhyphen{}pixel band is an example tolerance, not a universal constant. Planar scenes and pure rotation remain {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{degenerate cases}}}}; a plausible low residual alone does not prove a recoverable camera baseline.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Recover camera pose with calibration}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/essential:recover-camera-pose-with-calibration}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/essential:lec04-essential}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/essential::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A fundamental matrix works with pixels. Calibration removes each camera’s internal coordinate scaling, leaving a relation between \sphinxstylestrong{viewing directions}. That relation can reveal rotation and translation direction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} lecture PDF pages 22–23. The explicit SVD construction below is a computational companion to the slides’ essential\sphinxhyphen{}matrix and four\sphinxhyphen{}solution statements. OpenCV’s \sphinxhref{https://docs.opencv.org/4.12.0/d9/d0c/group\_\_calib3d.html}{official decomposition and pose\sphinxhyphen{}recovery documentation}%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
\sphinxnolinkurl{https://docs.opencv.org/4.12.0/d9/d0c/group\_\_calib3d.html}
%
\end{footnote} provides an implementation cross\sphinxhyphen{}check: four pose candidates, a translation direction, and a positive\sphinxhyphen{}depth test.

\index{Essential matrix@\spxentry{Essential matrix}!Cheirality; Translation scale@\spxentry{Cheirality; Translation scale}}\ignorespaces

\subsection{Remove intrinsics before asking about motion}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/essential:remove-intrinsics-before-asking-about-motion}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/essential:index-0}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the first camera as the reference: \(P=[I\mid0]\), \(P'=[R\mid t]\) in calibrated coordinates. Here \(X'=RX+t\); \sphinxstylestrong{\(t\) is a coordinate\sphinxhyphen{}transform translation}, and the second camera center in the first frame is \(-R^Tt\).

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — essential matrix and calibrated constraint}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/essential:eq-lec04-essential}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\widehat x&=K^{-1}x,\quad \widehat x'=K'^{-1}x',\\
E&=K'^TFK=[t]_\times R,\qquad \widehat x'^TE\widehat x=0,\\
[t]_\times&=\begin{pmatrix}0&-t_z&t_y\\t_z&0&-t_x\\-t_y&t_x&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K,K',F,E,R\) are \(3\times3\); \(t,\widehat x,\widehat x'\) are three\sphinxhyphen{}entry vectors. Use calibrated, undistorted coordinates and a nonzero baseline. \(E\) has five DOF: three for rotation and two for translation \sphinxstylestrong{direction}. A nonzero essential matrix has singular values \((a,a,0)\) with \(a>0\).

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Why does the constraint work? A 3D correspondence satisfies \(\lambda'\widehat x'=R\lambda\widehat x+t\). The vector \([t]_\times R\widehat x\) is perpendicular to both \(t\) and \(R\widehat x\), hence also to their combination \(\widehat x'\). Dotting them gives zero. Conversely, substituting calibrated coordinates into \(x'^TFx=0\) gives \(E=K'^TFK\).

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Separate calibration from coordinate normalization}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} valid \(F\) and both intrinsic matrices. Form \(E=K'^TFK\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check two equal nonzero singular values and a third zero, allowing measurement noise.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With noisy \(E=U\operatorname{diag}(s_1,s_2,s_3)V^T\), replace its singular values by \((a,a,0)\), where \(a=(s_1+s_2)/2\); require \(a>0\). This is the nearest essential\sphinxhyphen{}form correction in Frobenius norm.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Continue to pose decomposition and test positive depth.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K^{-1}\) removes camera intrinsics. The earlier \(T\) normalization only improves numerical conditioning. They serve different purposes. Unlike a general rank\sphinxhyphen{}two \(F\), an \(E\) also requires its first two singular values to agree.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Four algebraic poses, usually one visible scene}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/essential:four-algebraic-poses-usually-one-visible-scene}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — essential\sphinxhyphen{}matrix pose candidates}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/essential:eq-lec04-poses}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
E&\sim U\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)V^T,\qquad
W=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\\
R_1&=UWV^T,\quad R_2=UW^TV^T,\qquad
(R,t)\in\{(R_1,\pm u_3),(R_2,\pm u_3)\}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(u_3\) is the third column of \(U\). Choose SVD signs so \(\det U=\det V=+1\); flipping either third column leaves the zero\sphinxhyphen{}singular\sphinxhyphen{}value product unchanged. Then both \(R_i\) are proper rotations. The unit translation fixes an arbitrary scale, not a known physical baseline.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Choose a pose by cheirality}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Generate the four \((R,t)\) pairs and check \(R^TR=I\), \(\det R=1\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For each pair, solve \(\lambda'\widehat x'=R\lambda\widehat x+t\) for several reliable correspondences.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Keep the pose with positive depth in \sphinxstylestrong{both} cameras. This is \sphinxstylestrong{cheirality}: reconstructed points must lie in front of their observing cameras.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check reprojection errors. With noise, use many matches and inspect an ambiguous result rather than trusting one marginal point.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pure rotation, negligible parallax, or degenerate data can defeat this selection. General linear triangulation is developed in Lecture 6; the next example solves the two ray depths directly.

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/essential:ex-lec04-pose}}
\begin{TextbookBox}

\textbf{Two different singular\sphinxhyphen{}value rules}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
A fitted matrix has singular values \((3,2,0.1)\). A rank\sphinxhyphen{}two \(F\) correction keeps \((3,2,0)\). An essential\sphinxhyphen{}form correction uses \((2.5,2.5,0)\). The equal\sphinxhyphen{}pair condition is additional information supplied by calibration.

\end{TextbookBox}

\section{Stereo depth and its errors}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:stereo-depth-and-its-errors}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:lec04-stereo}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hold a finger in front of your face and close one eye at a time. Its apparent horizontal shift is larger when it is close. \sphinxstylestrong{Disparity} measures that shift in a rectified camera pair.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sources:} lecture PDF pages 58–64; Fall 2025 Quiz 3, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532f25\_quiz\_3\_solution.pdf}}, Q1–Q2, page 1; Spring 2019 Quiz 5, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s19\_quiz5\sphinxhyphen{}2.pdf}}, P1’s three bullets, page 1; Spring 2020 Quiz 5, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s20\_quiz5.pdf}}, same questions under an overprinted 2019/2020 header.

\index{Disparity@\spxentry{Disparity}!Stereo depth; Depth uncertainty@\spxentry{Stereo depth; Depth uncertainty}}\ignorespaces

\subsection{Turn horizontal shift into axial depth}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:turn-horizontal-shift-into-axial-depth}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:index-0}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assume aligned rectified cameras with a horizontal baseline \(b>0\), shared horizontal focal length \(f\) in pixels, and matched principal\sphinxhyphen{}point columns. Put the left center at \((0,0,0)\) and the right center at \((b,0,0)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a scene point \((X,Y,Z)\), the two horizontal projections obey
\(u_L-c_x=fX/Z\) and \(u_R-c_x=f(X-b)/Z\). Subtract them: \(u_L-u_R=fb/Z\).

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — rectified stereo depth}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/stereo:eq-lec04-depth}
\begin{split}d=u_L-u_R,\qquad Z=\frac{fb}{d}.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(f\) and \(d\) use pixels; \(Z\) uses the same length unit as \(b\). \(Z\) is axial depth. Require \(d>0\) under this camera order and forward\sphinxhyphen{}view convention. If principal\sphinxhyphen{}point columns differ, use corrected disparity \(d=(u_L-c_{xL})-(u_R-c_{xR})\) instead. A zero disparity is the ideal infinite\sphinxhyphen{}depth limit, not a finite reconstruction.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Reconstruct with a known baseline}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} rectified correspondence, calibrated pixel focal length, and baseline length.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check equal image rows and subtract horizontal coordinates in the stated order.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \(Z=fb/d\). Then use {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture01/cameras::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{calibrated backprojection}}}} if you also need \(X,Y\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check:} doubling disparity halves depth; doubling baseline at fixed disparity doubles depth. Keep centimeters and meters consistent.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The source’s BAD/GOOD rectification examples (PDF pages 59–60) illustrate that stereo needs compatible row alignment, not independently straightened pictures.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.900\linewidth]{{stereo-rays}.pdf}
\caption{A side view along the horizontal baseline: the difference between two projections fixes the ray intersection’s depth. Virtual image planes are drawn in front of the cameras.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:fig-lec04-stereo-rays}}\end{figure}


\subsection{A pixel error produces an asymmetric depth error}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:a-pixel-error-produces-an-asymmetric-depth-error}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the true disparity be \(d\) and the measured disparity \(d+\delta\). Define \sphinxstylestrong{signed error} as estimated depth minus true depth. Subtract the two depth fractions before approximating.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — exact and first\sphinxhyphen{}order depth error}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/stereo:eq-lec04-depth-error}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\Delta Z&=\frac{fb}{d+\delta}-\frac{fb}{d}
=-\frac{fb\,\delta}{d(d+\delta)},\\
\Delta Z&\approx-\frac{fb}{d^2}\delta\quad (|\delta|\ll d),\qquad
\frac{|\Delta Z|}{Z}\approx\frac{|\delta|}{d}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Require \(d>0\) and \(d+\delta>0\) for two finite forward\sphinxhyphen{}depth estimates. The approximation is the derivative of \(fb/d\) times \(\delta\). Its magnitude is often quoted without the minus sign; retain the sign when explaining whether the point moves nearer or farther.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Report uncertainty honestly}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} \(f,b,d\) and a signed disparity error \(\delta\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the true and estimated depths; subtract for an exact error.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the derivative only when \(|\delta|/d\) is small; label it an approximation.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check:} overestimating positive disparity makes depth too small. Underestimating it makes depth too large, by a larger magnitude for equal\sphinxhyphen{}size errors.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For bounded error \(|\delta|\le\epsilon<d\), the possible depths lie between \(fb/(d+\epsilon)\) and \(fb/(d-\epsilon)\). If the interval reaches zero disparity, there is no finite upper depth bound under this model.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{enumerate}

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Convert a permitted depth range into search limits}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:convert-a-permitted-depth-range-into-search-limits}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — disparity search from a depth interval}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/stereo:eq-lec04-disparity-range}
\begin{split}0<Z_{\min}\le Z\le Z_{\max}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{fb}{Z_{\max}}\le d\le\frac{fb}{Z_{\min}}.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The inequalities reverse because depth and positive disparity are inversely related. Use consistent length units and the corrected disparity convention when principal points differ.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Limit the stereo search}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Convert \(b,Z_{\min},Z_{\max}\) to the same length unit.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the continuous disparity endpoints.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For integer hypotheses inside that interval, use the ceiling of the lower endpoint and floor of the upper endpoint. If subpixel or calibration uncertainty matters, include an appropriate margin before discretizing.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check that the larger disparity belongs to the nearer depth.

\end{enumerate}

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:ex-lec04-search}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.8 — restrict the Fall 2025 search}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} Fall 2025 Quiz 3, Q2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \(b=0.1\,\mathrm m\), \(f=50\) pixels, and depth range \([1,5]\,\mathrm m\). Then \(fb=5\,\mathrm{m\,pixels}\), so \(d_{\min}=5/5=1\) pixel and \(d_{\max}=5/1=5\) pixels. Search integer disparities \(1,2,3,4,5\), or subpixel values in that interval.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a left column \(u_L\), candidates are at \(u_R=u_L-d\) on the matching row. Also clip the search to valid image coordinates; a geometrically permitted match can still fall outside the image.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Find matches across an image}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:find-matches-across-an-image}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:lec04-matching}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Geometry narrows the search to a row. \sphinxstylestrong{Appearance chooses a position along it.} That is still difficult: repeated textures can look identical, flat regions have little evidence, and some pixels are visible in only one camera.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} lecture PDF pages 42–77, printed slides 46–81 except unnumbered PDF page 54. Stereo contributors named on PDF page 42: Rick Szeliski, Pascal Fua, P. Mordohai, and E. Dunn.


\subsection{Generate, evaluate, select}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:generate-evaluate-select}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The slide sequence on pages 45–53 follows one practical pipeline:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Generate hypotheses:} sample possible disparities or depths. Each projects the reference pixel to a candidate in another view.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Evaluate:} compare image appearance at the candidate, then combine neighboring evidence.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Select:} choose a supported hypothesis, or reject the pixel when evidence is unreliable.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstylestrong{cost volume} stores one score for each image position and hypothesis: dimensions width × height × number of disparities. A depth map selects one hypothesis per reference pixel; it is view\sphinxhyphen{}dependent and need not contain occluded surfaces. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture01/motivation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{earlier reconstruction pipeline}}}} explains how depth can feed other 3D representations.

\index{Cost volume@\spxentry{Cost volume}!Photo\sphinxhyphen{}consistency; Occlusion@\spxentry{Photo\sphinxhyphen{}consistency; Occlusion}}\ignorespaces
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — aggregate costs and select disparity}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/matching:eq-lec04-cost-volume}
\begin{split}\overline C(p,d)=\frac1{|\Omega_p|}\sum_{q\in\Omega_p}C(q,d),
\qquad \widehat d(p)\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{d\in D_p}\overline C(p,d).\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(p,q\) are pixel positions, \(D_p\) the allowed disparity set, and \(\Omega_p\) a support window. \(C(q,d)\) is a dissimilarity between left location \(q\) and right location \(q-(d,0)\). Require valid samples and nonempty support. An argmin can contain several disparities: a tie is evidence of ambiguity, not a unique measurement.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Build a simple dense stereo estimate}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} rectified images and the permitted disparity range.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Evaluate a cost at every valid candidate. Stack these candidate costs into the volume.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Aggregate support and pick the smallest cost; retain a confidence measure such as separation from competing minima.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Reject inconsistent left–right matches and occlusions. Convert reliable disparities to depth.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is \sphinxstylestrong{winner\sphinxhyphen{}take\sphinxhyphen{}all} selection. The slides also name feature/edge matching followed by interpolation and joint optimization using iterative updates, dynamic programming, energy minimization, or graph methods. Those alternatives add spatial reasoning; they do not make missing image evidence appear.

\end{TextbookBox}

\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.900\linewidth]{{stereo-pair}.pdf}
\caption{The actual reference/matching photographs from PDF page 46, printed slide 50. Look at the toy and leaf boundaries: viewpoints change which surfaces are visible. Extracted photographs with original project labels; individual photography credits and reuse terms are not identified on the slide.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:fig-lec04-pair}}\end{figure}


\subsection{Compare patches, not isolated colors}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:compare-patches-not-isolated-colors}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Photo\sphinxhyphen{}consistency} means that projections of the same scene point have compatible image appearance under the chosen model. For a patch, write its paired samples as \(L_i,R_i(d)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\).

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — SAD, SSD, and zero\sphinxhyphen{}mean NCC}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/matching:eq-lec04-patch-costs}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{SAD}(d)&=\sum_i|L_i-R_i(d)|,\qquad
\operatorname{SSD}(d)=\sum_i(L_i-R_i(d))^2,\\
\operatorname{NCC}(d)&=
\frac{\sum_i(L_i-\overline L)(R_i(d)-\overline R(d))}
{\sqrt{\sum_i(L_i-\overline L)^2\sum_i(R_i(d)-\overline R(d))^2}}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\overline L,\overline R\) are patch means. Minimize SAD/SSD; \sphinxstylestrong{maximize} NCC, or minimize a cost such as \(1-\operatorname{NCC}\). NCC lies in \([-1,1]\) for nonconstant patches and is undefined if either centered patch has zero norm. SAD uses intensity units, SSD squared intensity units, NCC is dimensionless.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Choose and check a patch score}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the same valid support and disparity convention for each candidate.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For SAD/SSD, compare aligned intensities directly. SSD penalizes large differences more strongly.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For NCC, subtract each patch’s own mean and divide by its centered norm. Reject near\sphinxhyphen{}zero\sphinxhyphen{}variance supports.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inspect the full score curve: multiple similar peaks or minima indicate uncertainty.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Positive affine brightness changes preserve ideal NCC, but clipping, reflections, shadows, and nonuniform exposure can break that assumption. The source’s formula image leaves normalization factors dependent on its standard\sphinxhyphen{}deviation convention; the explicit sum\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}squares denominator above avoids that ambiguity.

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:ex-lec04-patches}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.9 — when raw intensity picks the wrong patch}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Original companion to:} PDF pages 65–70.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reference \(L=(10,20,30)\) has two candidate patches: true but brighter \(R_A=(30,40,50)\), and wrong \(R_B=(10,20,10)\).

&

\sphinxAtStartPar
Raw difference scores favor B. For NCC, A’s centered values equal the reference’s \((-10,0,10)\), giving correlation one. B’s centered values are \((-10/3,20/3,-10/3)\), perpendicular to the reference vector, giving zero. NCC favors A under the uniform brightness\sphinxhyphen{}offset model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A flat patch such as \((20,20,20)\) instead has zero centered norm. It cannot supply a defined NCC score or a distinctive texture match.

\subsection{Window size trades detail for support}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:window-size-trades-detail-for-support}}
\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.850\linewidth]{{window-size}.png}
\caption{The source’s \(w=3\) versus \(w=20\) results, left to right (PDF page 66, printed slide 70). Larger support suppresses isolated mistakes but can erase detail. Extracted source illustration; its individual creator and reuse terms are not identified on that slide.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:fig-lec04-window-size}}\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A constant\sphinxhyphen{}disparity window assumes \sphinxstylestrong{fronto\sphinxhyphen{}parallel support}: one axial depth. Slanted surfaces violate this assumption; windows crossing foreground and background mix different depths.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.850\linewidth]{{support-boundary}.pdf}
\caption{A larger window can vote for two different depths. Adapting its position or weights changes which surface contributes evidence.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:fig-lec04-support}}\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The slides offer several ways to adapt support:
\begin{itemize}
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Shiftable windows:} choose among windows that contain the reference pixel; favor support that stays on one surface.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Rod\sphinxhyphen{}shaped supports:} test elongated directions that may follow an approximately constant\sphinxhyphen{}disparity contour.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adaptive weights:} downweight neighbors far away in position or color.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Oriented\sphinxhyphen{}plane hypotheses:} allow disparity to vary across a slanted plane instead of assuming one constant value.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All add assumptions. Similar colors can still occur at different depths, and an image edge need not be a depth edge.


\subsection{Rank and Census use relative intensity order}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:rank-and-census-use-relative-intensity-order}}
\index{Census transform@\spxentry{Census transform}!Rank transform; Adaptive support@\spxentry{Rank transform; Adaptive support}}\ignorespaces
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — rank, Census, and Hamming distance}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/matching:eq-lec04-census}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
r(p)&=\sum_{q\in\mathcal N_p}\mathbf1[I(q)<I(p)],\\
\mathcal C(p)&=\bigl(\mathbf1[I(q_1)<I(p)],\ldots,
\mathbf1[I(q_m)<I(p)]\bigr),\\
H(\mathcal C_L,\mathcal C_R)&=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf1[\mathcal C_{L,i}\ne\mathcal C_{R,i}].
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\mathcal N_p\) contains \(m\) ordered neighbors excluding the center; \(\mathbf1[\cdot]\) is one when its condition is true and zero otherwise. Rank ranges from \(0\) to \(m\); Census keeps the complete ordered bit string. Use the same neighbor order and tie convention in both images. Both preserve strictly increasing intensity remappings within the compared support.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Match relative\sphinxhyphen{}intensity patterns}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare each neighbor with the center using the fixed strict inequality.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sum the comparisons for rank, or retain their order for Census.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare rank\sphinxhyphen{}transformed images with a difference cost; compare Census strings by Hamming distance.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check for repeated patterns and ties. Relative order is robust to some brightness changes, not to all lighting or geometry changes.

\end{enumerate}

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:ex-lec04-census}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.10 — equal ranks can hide different patterns}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Original companion to:} PDF page 74, printed slide 78.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the center intensity be 20. Ordered neighbors \((10,30,15,25)\) give Census \sphinxstylestrong{1010} and rank 2. A second patch with center 20 and neighbors \((5,10,30,40)\) gives \sphinxstylestrong{1100}, also rank 2. Their Census Hamming distance is \sphinxstylestrong{2}: bits 2 and 3 disagree.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rank compresses spatial evidence into one count. Census retains which neighbors were darker. Adding the same brightness offset to every pixel of either patch preserves its comparisons, provided clipping does not change them.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Give nearby, similar neighbors more influence}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:give-nearby-similar-neighbors-more-influence}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — locally adaptive support}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/matching:eq-lec04-adaptive}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\Delta_c(p,q)&=\|\operatorname{Lab}(p)-\operatorname{Lab}(q)\|_2,
\quad \Delta_s(p,q)=\|p-q\|_2,\\
w(p,q)&=\exp\left[-\frac{\Delta_c(p,q)}{\gamma_c}
-\frac{\Delta_s(p,q)}{\gamma_s}\right],\\
\overline C_w(p,d)&=\frac{\sum_{q\in\Omega_p}w(p,q)C(q,d)}
{\sum_{q\in\Omega_p}w(p,q)}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\gamma_c,\gamma_s>0\) set color and spatial scales; \(\gamma_s\) uses pixels. The exponential arguments are dimensionless. This displayed version uses reference\sphinxhyphen{}image weights and requires a nonzero weight sum. Some methods also incorporate shifted right\sphinxhyphen{}image weights; state the convention rather than mixing implementations. A constant multiplier in every weight cancels in the normalized cost.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Aggregate without crossing every edge equally}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute color distance in CIE Lab and spatial distance within the support.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate positive weights with the chosen scales.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Form a weighted average cost for each disparity and compare candidates.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inspect whether the support follows actual surfaces. Color similarity helps; it does not prove shared depth.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
PDF pages 52/76 credit Yoon and Kweon (PAMI 2006); page 53 credits Lu et al. (CVPR 2013) for an oriented\sphinxhyphen{}plane extension. These descriptions explain their roles; they do not reproduce the full methods.

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:ex-lec04-adaptive}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.11 — a two\sphinxhyphen{}sample depth boundary}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Original companion to:} PDF pages 75–76.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two support samples are each one pixel away. One has the same color as the reference; the other differs by 40 Lab units. With \(\gamma_c=10\), \(\gamma_s=2\), their weights are \(e^{-0.5}\approx0.60653\) and \(e^{-4.5}\approx0.01111\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the true disparity, their costs are \((0,10)\); at a wrong disparity, \((10,0)\). Uniform averaging ties both at 5. Adaptive averaging gives about \sphinxstylestrong{0.180} for the true disparity and \sphinxstylestrong{9.820} for the wrong one. The same\sphinxhyphen{}color sample now contributes most of the evidence.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If that color boundary did not correspond to a depth boundary, this weighting preference could be misleading. The source’s result images compare such support choices, not a universal guarantee of correctness.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The slide list also names \sphinxstylestrong{mutual information} (statistical dependence between intensities) and \sphinxstylestrong{learning\sphinxhyphen{}based methods} (learned appearance features or costs). They change how hypotheses are scored. The same geometry, visibility limits, and need to recognize uncertain matches remain.

\section{TLDR}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:tldr}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Lecture 4 in one sentence:} estimate valid two\sphinxhyphen{}view geometry, choose a camera pose that sees the scene, and turn reliable stereo matches into depths with honest error estimates.


\subsection{The important things}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:the-important-things}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Keep points, lines, and scalars distinct.} The assigned quizzes apply the existing epipolar rules to symbolic expansion and third\sphinxhyphen{}view prediction. Two lines in a third image can locate a point, unless their intersection is degenerate. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{quiz practice}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check rank before trusting “F.”} Fall 2025 Quiz 2 supplies a rank\sphinxhyphen{}three matrix. Its bilinear equation can be solved, but it is not valid pinhole\sphinxhyphen{}camera geometry. A noisy estimate requires a rank\sphinxhyphen{}two correction and pixel\sphinxhyphen{}space residual checks. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{estimation}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Calibration supplies an essential matrix.} \(E=K'^TFK=[t]_\times R\) has equal nonzero singular values and one zero. It recovers translation direction, not metric scale. Numerical conditioning transforms and camera calibration are different operations. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/essential::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{essential geometry}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Test all four poses.} Two rotations and two translation signs produce four candidates. Positive reconstructed depths in both cameras select the visible configuration for suitable nondegenerate data. Translation \(t\) is not the second camera center.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Disparity is inverse depth.} In the specified rectified convention, \(Z=fb/d\). Use focal length and disparity in pixels, baseline and depth in one length unit. Account for unequal principal\sphinxhyphen{}point columns. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{stereo}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A one\sphinxhyphen{}pixel depth error is not symmetric.} Underestimating disparity pushes the point farther by more than an equal overestimate pulls it nearer. Use the exact error when the disparity error is a substantial fraction of disparity. Small disparities are especially fragile.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Appearance chooses among geometric candidates.} Dense stereo generates hypotheses, evaluates costs, aggregates support, and selects or rejects. Minimize SAD/SSD; maximize NCC. Flat patches, repetitions, and occlusions can defeat a low\sphinxhyphen{}cost match. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{matching}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Support has assumptions.} A constant\sphinxhyphen{}disparity window favors fronto\sphinxhyphen{}parallel surfaces; large windows can mix depths. Shifted, elongated, weighted, or oriented\sphinxhyphen{}plane support can help. Rank retains a count; Census retains the ordered relative\sphinxhyphen{}intensity pattern. None removes ambiguity automatically.

\end{enumerate}

\newpage


\subsection{Short quiz}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:short-quiz}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These original questions test this chapter’s additions.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(x_A=(0,1,1)^T\), \(x_B=(1,0,1)^T\), expand \(x_B^TFx_A\) in matrix entries.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Two predicted lines in image C are proportional. Does their cross product give a unique finite correspondence?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A noisy matrix has singular values \((4,2,0.2)\). What singular values do rank\sphinxhyphen{}two F correction and essential\sphinxhyphen{}form correction use?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A candidate pose reconstructs a point with depths \(+5\) and \(-5\) in the two cameras. Is that point a valid visible correspondence under that pose?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rectified cameras have \(b=0.2\,\mathrm m\), \(f=600\) pixels, \(d=30\) pixels. What is the depth? If measured disparity becomes 31, is the point reconstructed nearer or farther?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For that setup, which disparity interval corresponds to depths from 2 to 6 meters?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Which direction do you optimize SAD and NCC? Can a constant\sphinxhyphen{}intensity patch supply a defined zero\sphinxhyphen{}mean NCC score?

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With center intensity 10 and ordered neighbors \((8,12,7,11)\), what are the Census string and rank under the strict darker\sphinxhyphen{}than\sphinxhyphen{}center convention?

\end{enumerate}


\subsection{Answers}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:answers}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Show answers and short explanations}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\(f_{12}+f_{13}+f_{32}+f_{33}=0\).} The right vector selects columns 2 and 3; the left vector selects rows 1 and 3.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{No.} Proportional line vectors describe the same line. Their cross product is zero, so a unique point is undetermined.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{F: \((4,2,0)\); E: \((3,3,0)\).} E additionally requires its first two singular values to agree.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{No.} The point is behind the second camera. Positive depth is required in both observing cameras.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{4 meters; nearer.} The perturbed estimate is \(120/31\approx3.871\,\mathrm m\), giving signed error \(-4/31\approx-0.129\,\mathrm m\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\([20,60]\) pixels.} The far endpoint gives \(120/6\); the near endpoint gives \(120/2\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Minimize SAD, maximize NCC; no.} A flat patch has zero centered norm, making NCC’s denominator zero.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{1010; rank 2.} Neighbors 1 and 3 are darker. Census keeps their positions, while rank keeps only their count.

\end{enumerate}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
